name: Sample Test (original questions)
source: Original practice questions written for LSAT Trainer. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: City council member: Last year, the neighborhoods that installed new streetlights saw a 20 percent drop in reported burglaries. Therefore, installing new streetlights in every neighborhood of the city will reduce burglaries citywide.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the council member's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: takes for granted that burglary is the most serious crime in the city
relies on evidence from a source whose impartiality is open to question
draws a conclusion about the cost of streetlights from evidence about their effectiveness
presumes, without providing justification, that the neighborhoods that installed streetlights are representative of the city's other neighborhoods
treats the number of burglaries in a neighborhood as though it were the same as the number of burglars
questions.explanation: The argument generalizes from the neighborhoods that chose streetlights to every neighborhood. If those neighborhoods differ (e.g., they had a lighting problem the others don't), the result may not carry over.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: The Varran wetland's population of marsh frogs has declined sharply over the past decade. A fungal disease that is often fatal to marsh frogs was first detected in the wetland ten years ago. The disease, therefore, is probably responsible for the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the ecologist's argument depends?
choices: The fungal disease is the only threat to marsh frogs in the wetland.
The fungal disease kills marsh frogs in numbers large enough to affect the size of the wetland's population.
Most marsh frogs that contract the disease die within a year of infection.
No other amphibian species in the wetland has declined over the past decade.
The fungal disease will eventually eliminate the wetland's marsh frog population.
questions.explanation: Negate B: the disease kills too few frogs to affect the population. Then it cannot explain the decline, and the argument collapses. A, C, and E are stronger than the argument needs; D is irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Nutritionist: Children who eat breakfast every day score higher, on average, on standardized tests than children who do not. So eating breakfast improves children's test performance.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the nutritionist's argument?
choices: Children who eat breakfast every day also tend to get more sleep than children who do not.
Children who eat breakfast every day tend to come from households with higher incomes than children who do not.
Some children who regularly skip breakfast score well above average on standardized tests.
Standardized tests are administered in the morning in most school districts.
In a study in which randomly selected children were given breakfast at school, their test scores rose relative to those of a similar group of children who were not given breakfast.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from correlation to causation. A randomized study isolates breakfast as the cause. B and A raise alternative causes (weakeners).

questions.stimulus: Manager: Since we began allowing employees to work from home two days per week, the number of reports our department completes each month has increased by 15 percent. Clearly, the remote-work policy has made our employees more productive.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the manager's argument?
choices: Other departments that adopted similar policies also saw increases in output.
Employees report greater job satisfaction since the policy began.
When the policy began, the department also hired several new employees, increasing its staff by 20 percent.
A few employees chose to continue working in the office five days per week.
The reports completed since the policy began are about the same length as those completed before it.
questions.explanation: Productivity is output per employee. Staff grew 20% while output grew only 15%, so output per employee actually fell. E rules out an alternative explanation, which strengthens.

questions.stimulus: All of the paintings in the gallery's east wing were acquired before 1950. Any painting acquired before 1950 has been professionally restored at least once. Therefore, the Ravel landscape has been professionally restored at least once.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The Ravel landscape is in the gallery's east wing.
The Ravel landscape was acquired after 1950.
Every painting that has been professionally restored was acquired before 1950.
Some paintings in the east wing have been restored more than once.
The Ravel landscape has never been displayed outside the gallery.
questions.explanation: Chain: east wing → acquired before 1950 → restored. Placing the Ravel in the east wing completes the chain. C reverses the second conditional.

questions.stimulus: Most of the novelists who won the Harlan Prize in the past twenty years had previously published at least three books. However, none of the novelists who won the prize in that period had previously won any other major literary award.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: No novelist who has won another major literary award has published three or more books.
At least some novelists who had published three or more books won the Harlan Prize without having previously won another major literary award.
The Harlan Prize is not considered a major literary award.
Most novelists who have published at least three books have won the Harlan Prize.
Novelists who win the Harlan Prize rarely win other major literary awards afterward.
questions.explanation: Most winners had 3+ books, and all winners lacked prior awards, so at least some 3+-book novelists won without prior awards. D reverses 'most'; E is about later awards, which the stimulus never mentions.

questions.stimulus: In an experiment, participants who were told that a wine was expensive rated it as tasting better than did participants who tasted the same wine but were told it was inexpensive. Brain imaging showed that regions associated with pleasure were more active in participants who were told the wine was expensive.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Price is the most important factor in consumers' choices of wine.
Expensive wines generally taste better than inexpensive wines.
Most people cannot distinguish between wines on the basis of taste alone.
Participants who were told the wine was expensive misreported their ratings.
Beliefs about a product can affect how pleasurable the experience of consuming it is.
questions.explanation: Same wine, different beliefs, different ratings and different brain activity. E says only 'can', which is all the evidence supports. C and A are too strong; D contradicts the imaging evidence.

questions.stimulus: To reduce accidents, the town of Delford installed a traffic light at its busiest intersection. In the year following the installation, however, the number of accidents at that intersection increased.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The traffic light was installed at a lower cost than the town had anticipated.
Traffic lights have reduced accidents at busy intersections in many other towns.
Shortly after the light was installed, a new highway exit opened nearby, and traffic through the intersection more than doubled.
Most drivers in Delford approve of the new traffic light.
The number of accidents at Delford's other intersections remained stable during that year.
questions.explanation: If traffic doubled, the accident count can rise even if the light lowered the accident rate. B deepens the puzzle instead of resolving it.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The new museum's design has been widely praised for its bold use of glass. Yet a building whose primary purpose is to protect fragile artworks should not admit so much sunlight, which fades pigments. The architects, therefore, failed at the most important part of their task, however striking the result may be.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the critic's argument?
choices: A building that protects fragile artworks should not admit much sunlight.
The museum's design has been widely praised for its bold use of glass.
Sunlight fades the pigments of fragile artworks.
The architects failed at the most important part of their task.
The new museum's design is visually striking.
questions.explanation: 'Therefore' marks the conclusion. A is a premise that supports it, and B is background that the critic argues against.

questions.stimulus:
Alicia: Public libraries should eliminate late fees. Such fees deter many low-income patrons from borrowing books at all.

Benjamin: But without late fees, patrons would have little reason to return books promptly, and other patrons would wait longer for popular titles.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Alicia and Benjamin disagree over whether
choices: public libraries should eliminate late fees
late fees deter low-income patrons from borrowing books
popular titles are in high demand at public libraries
patrons would return books promptly in the absence of late fees
public libraries depend on late fees for a significant part of their revenue
questions.explanation: Alicia endorses eliminating fees; Benjamin's 'But' objects to it. Benjamin never addresses B, and Alicia never addresses D, so neither is a point of disagreement.

passages.title: Dendrochronology and panel paintings
passages.text:
For centuries, art historians attributed and dated Northern European panel paintings chiefly by stylistic analysis—comparing brushwork, composition, and iconography with those of securely documented works. Such judgments, however expert, are inherently contestable, and disputes over whether a panel was painted by a master or by a later imitator could persist for generations. Over the past several decades, dendrochronology, the dating of wood by the pattern of its annual growth rings, has offered a means of anchoring these debates in physical evidence.

Many such paintings were executed on oak panels, and because the width of an oak's annual rings varies with climatic conditions, a sequence of rings from a panel can be matched against regional master chronologies compiled from timbers of known date. When the match is secure, the analyst can identify the year in which the outermost surviving ring grew. Yet that year is not the date of the painting. Panel makers trimmed away the sapwood—the outer, softer rings—and the wood was typically seasoned for some years before use. Analysts therefore estimate an earliest plausible date of creation by adding a statistically derived allowance for missing sapwood and a minimum seasoning period.

The resulting date establishes when a painting could first have been made, not when it was made. Dendrochronology thus excels at exclusion. A panel whose wood was felled decades after a master's death cannot be that master's work, whatever its stylistic merits. But a panel whose dating is consistent with an attribution does not thereby confirm it, since imitators active in the same period would have drawn on the same timber supplies. The technique, in short, does not replace connoisseurship; it disciplines it, narrowing the range of hypotheses that stylistic analysis must adjudicate.
passages.subject: humanities

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Dendrochronology has rendered stylistic analysis obsolete as a method of attributing panel paintings.
Dendrochronology provides physical evidence that can rule out some attributions of panel paintings, although it cannot by itself confirm them.
Because panel makers removed sapwood, dendrochronological dates for panel paintings are unreliable.
Disputes over the attribution of Northern European panel paintings have persisted because of the limitations of stylistic analysis.
Regional master chronologies allow analysts to determine the exact year in which a panel painting was created.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph states the thesis: the technique excels at exclusion but does not replace connoisseurship. A contradicts the final sentence, and E contradicts paragraph two.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the allowance that analysts add to the date of the outermost surviving ring reflects which one of the following?
choices: rings removed when the sapwood was trimmed, together with the time the wood was seasoned
variations in climatic conditions across different regions
the time a painter typically required to complete a panel painting
errors that occur in compiling regional master chronologies
the period during which imitators of a master were active
questions.explanation: Paragraph two: the allowance covers the missing sapwood and a minimum seasoning period.

questions.stem: Which one of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage about a panel painting whose dendrochronological dating is consistent with its attribution to a particular master?
choices: It was painted by that master.
It was painted before that master's death.
It could nonetheless have been painted by an imitator of that master.
Its stylistic features resemble those of the master's documented works.
Its wood was seasoned for longer than was typical.
questions.explanation: A consistent date does not confirm the attribution because imitators used the same timber, so the panel could still be an imitator's work. B overstates what an earliest-possible date shows.

questions.stem: The author mentions imitators active in the same period primarily in order to
choices: show that dendrochronology can identify the work of imitators
suggest that most disputed panel paintings were in fact painted by imitators
illustrate the expertise that stylistic analysis requires
argue that timber suitable for panels was scarce during the period
explain why a dendrochronological date consistent with an attribution does not confirm that attribution
questions.explanation: The reference is the 'since' clause supporting the claim that consistency does not confirm an attribution.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the use of dendrochronology in attributing panel paintings is best described as
choices: indifference to its methodological details
skepticism that it adds anything to stylistic analysis
enthusiasm for its ability to settle attribution disputes conclusively
appreciation of its value, tempered by recognition of its limits
disapproval of its growing use by art historians
questions.explanation: 'Excels at exclusion' and 'disciplines' connoisseurship are positive, while 'does not thereby confirm it' marks a limit.
